title: the story every Passover retells in first person
hook: the story every Passover retells in first person
tomorrow: "we will do and we will hear"

segments.voice: Yesterday: tzedakah. Justice, not charity, one coin at a time. Your line was give before you feel like it. Did you give something before the feeling caught up? Day eleven.
screen: `TZEDAKAH — GIVE BEFORE YOU FEEL LIKE IT.`

segments.voice: It's a spring night, and a long table is crowded with plates that don't match, borrowed chairs, a cousin you see once a year. On the table: flat crackers, a bowl of salt water, bitter herbs, a roasted bone. The youngest child stands up, a little nervous, and asks a question in a sing-song everyone knows: why is this night different from all other nights? And the grown-ups answer. Not with "once upon a time." Not with "our ancestors." They answer with one word: we. Today: the story every Passover retells, and why it's told as if it happened to you.
screen: `A LONG TABLE, A SPRING NIGHT.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?` → `THE ANSWER STARTS WITH WE.`

segments.voice: The Exodus is the going out: the story in the book of Exodus of the Israelites enslaved in Egypt, a Pharaoh who fears them, a baby in a basket who grows up to be Moses, ten plagues, a night of leaving in such a hurry the bread has no time to rise, and a sea that opens. It's the story Judaism keeps returning to more than any other. The prayers mention it every day. The Sabbath commandment remembers it, as we saw on day seven. But at Passover it isn't only remembered. It's retold, around a table, following a little book called the Haggadah, which means the telling. The Torah itself commands the telling. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." For me. When I came out. And so the answer to the child's question begins with a line drawn from Deuteronomy: we were Pharaoh's slaves in Egypt. The Mishnah makes it a rule: in every generation, a person must see themselves as if they personally came out of Egypt. Not a history lesson. A memory you're invited into. And it turns into ethics. The Torah repeats one command about the stranger more often than almost anything else: "And a stranger shalt thou not wrong, neither shalt thou oppress him; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." You know what it's like, the text says. You were there. So when someone is the outsider now, remember which side of the story you were on.
screen: `THE GOING OUT OF EGYPT.` · `THE HAGGADAH — THE TELLING.` · `AS IF YOU CAME OUT YOURSELF.` · `YOU WERE STRANGERS. REMEMBER.` · then, large: `WE WERE SLAVES.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Remember a time you were the outsider: the new kid, the one who didn't speak the language, the one who didn't know the rules. Feel it again, just a little. Then think of someone who's the outsider in your life right now. Hold both of them, the old you and that person, together. The bell holds the time.
The Exodus. The going out of Egypt, retold every Passover in the first person, as if it happened to you. Eleventh word.
Your line: we were slaves. Today, do one kind thing for someone who's new, or foreign, or on the outside, because you remember what that was like. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "WE WILL DO AND WE WILL HEAR."`

howItsDone: At Passover, Jewish families hold a seder, reading the Haggadah around the table: the youngest asks the four questions, the story of the Exodus is told in the first person, and matzah, bitter herbs and salt water are eaten as part of the telling.

original.note: Hebrew: the going out of Egypt, the phrase Jewish prayer uses for the Exodus.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old story about Moses and a sea.
what it means: the story Judaism returns to most, retold every year in the first person: we were slaves.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 13:8 commands the telling 'for me'; Mishnah Pesachim 10:5 makes every generation see itself as leaving Egypt; the stranger laws ground ethics in that memory.

notes: Exodus 22:20 is JPS 1917 numbering (KJV 22:21); confirm exact wording.
'Repeats one command about the stranger more often than almost anything else' reflects the rabbinic count (Bava Metzia 59b: 36 or 46 times); stated loosely. Confirm.
'Why is this night different from all other nights?' given as a common English form of the Ma Nishtanah, not as a quotation of a translation; confirm.
Fork setup originally said the story is 'some three thousand years old'; softened to 'ancient' because the dating and historicity of the Exodus are debated.
Mishnah Pesachim 10:5 paraphrased with gender-neutral 'themselves'; confirm acceptable.
